## 4. `shading.js` — the shared material patch

`createShading(THREE)` returns `{ apply, update, reset, ... }`. Every material in the game (terrain, props, trail, rider, huts, wildlife, helicopter) goes through `apply` — there is no unpatched path on purpose.

**`apply(material, opts)`** installs an `onBeforeCompile` and:
- **calls any pre-existing `onBeforeCompile` first** and keeps its edits (this is the contract props.js/terrain.js lean on);
- `Object.assign(shader.uniforms, uniforms, own)` — **shared uniform objects by reference**, so one write per frame in `update()` moves fog/sky/sun across six modules that know nothing about each other;
- patches vertex: `common` → `VERT_PARS` (`varying vec3 vN64View; varying float vN64Ice, vN64Sheen;`), `project_vertex` → keeps `mvPosition.xyz` (geometry is never snapped — the old vertex-snap/light-banding retro treatment was retired);
- patches fragment at four anchors, each guarded by an `indexOf` check so unlit materials silently skip:
  - `lights_fragment_maps` → **`FRAG_SHADE`**: the mountain's own horizon shadow, a *world-aligned toroidal* atlas (5×5 tiles, 480 m modulo) marched by terrain.js — so a tree at the foot of the containment wall is shadowed by the wall even though the depth map doesn't hold the mountain;
  - `lights_fragment_end` → **`lightPatch(sheen)`** = `FRAG_SUN` + `FRAG_RECOVER` + `FRAG_SHEEN`. `FRAG_RECOVER` **divides the shadow back out of `directDiffuse`** (`albedo·dotNL·sunRadiance·shadow/π`, everything but shadow is in scope) instead of doing a second PCF lookup. `FRAG_SHEEN` is a GGX microfacet snow response — `SHEEN.f0 = 0.018` (real ice), roughness from a snowpack field (`vN64Ice`), Schlick Fresnel to reflected sky at grazing angles, and a wrapped subsurface term. Gated by a luminance mask (`SNOW_LO 0.22 / SNOW_HI 0.42`) times `uSheen` times per-vertex `vN64Sheen`, so rock and everything that never asked skip the expensive second sky evaluation;
  - `fog_fragment` → **`FRAG_FOG`**: three's fog is disabled (`material.fog = false`) and replaced by directional aerial perspective — `mix(colour, n64Sky(viewDir), smoothstep(fogNear, fogFar, dist * uFogPull))` plus a height-based valley-mist term that blends to the flat haze stop (never the directional gradient — routing it through the sun lobe turned golden-hour slopes mud-brown). Branch-skipped when `fog < 0.003`;
  - `alphamap_fragment` → **`FRAG_CAMERA_FADE`**: `diffuseColor.a *= smoothstep(2.2, 6.5, length(vN64View))` + `material.alphaHash = true`, so the chase camera inside a conifer screen-doors it away without sorting errors.
- **`uFogPull`** is the notable per-material knob: how much *further away* a surface pretends to be when asking the curtain. Snow is already haze-coloured and vanishes at f≈0.5; a dark crown needs f≈0.95 — without this the ground dissolves out from under a forest that doesn't. Props pass `FOG_PULL_TREE/STONE/FLORA`.
- **`customProgramCacheKey`** is mandatory here and explained: three's default key is the *text* of `onBeforeCompile`, and every patched material shares one closure with identical text, so without a key the terrain and the trees would collide on one program. The key encodes the patches requested plus `prev.toString()`.
- `SKY_GLSL` is exported and included by **both** the dome material and every lit material's fog term — the cloud deck is a ray/plane intersection (4 instructions) sampled in a wrapping 64-cell procedural noise field, written to keep operands `mediump`-honest. A separate `n64SkyReflect` is the same sky *without* the cloud octaves, for the rough snow reflection.
- `createCloudShadowTexture` bakes 3 periodic value-noise octaves into a 128×128 `RedFormat` DataTexture (16 KiB) — one filtered read per fragment gives every material the same cloud shadow.

Other `onBeforeCompile` patches in props.js: `treeMat` / `floraMat` / `rockMat` add **triplanar textures** in `color_fragment` (bark ×3 axes weighted by `abs(normal)`, needles by world xz, `step(0.35, diffuseColor.g)` picks bark vs needle), `alpineMat` maps wood planks, `lampMat`/`pisteStakeLampMat` are unlit `MeshBasicMaterial` with `toneMapped = false` whose `color_vertex` is replaced by `BEACON`/`PISTE_BEACON` — a flash that is a pure function of `uAirTime`, phase from `instanceMatrix[3].z` (so both poles of a gate flash together and consecutive gates ripple), and `uNextGate` promotes the leader with a faster clock and 2× output. Lamps keep three's fog so a beacon still dies in a whiteout.

## 5. `hud.js` + `font.js` — the retro 5×7 bitmap read-out

### `font.js` (276 lines)
- Each glyph is **5 columns × 7 bits**, bit 0 = top row (the HD44780 convention). `GLYPH_W 5, GLYPH_H 7, ADVANCE 6, LINE 9`. Monospace on purpose — tabular figures by not having any other kind.
- `GLYPHS` is a flat `{char: [5 bytes]}` table: A–Z, 0–9, and exactly the punctuation the HUD speaks (`. , : · + × — - ° / % ( ) [ ] < > ◀ ▶ ▲ ▼ ✦ ← Ⅱ ♪`). Missing glyphs draw `TOFU` (a hollow box), never a space.
- **Halo/outline**: derived by bit dilation, not by drawing 8 times. `smeared[i] = c | c<<1 | c>>1` (vertical), then each halo column ORs its two neighbours (horizontal) → a 7×9 bitmap, cached in `halos: Map`. Because advance (6) > ink (5), a halo occupies the air column and never touches a neighbour's ink — which is what makes one-pass-per-string safe.
- **Sprite cache**: each `(char, size, colour, halo)` is baked once into its own offscreen canvas (halo pass then ink pass) and every subsequent appearance is one `drawImage` at integer coords and native scale. `column()` emits vertical *runs* as `fillRect`s (≈8 rects/glyph instead of 35). `SPRITE_LIMIT = 384`, cleared wholesale when full.
- API: `drawText(ctx, str, x, y, colour, size = 1, halo = null)` (upper-cases on the way in, skips spaces, returns the width) and `measure(str, size)` (doesn't count the trailing air column).

### `hud.js` (910 lines)
- A **second canvas** (`.readout`, `aria-hidden`) sized to the *display*, not the adaptive 3D target, so text stays sharp when the GPU lowers world resolution. `ctx.imageSmoothingEnabled = false`; everything lands on whole buffer pixels.
- **Scale in whole stops only**: `UI = min(round(H / LINES_PER_STOP=400), floor(min(W/FOOT_W, H/FOOT_H)), UI_MAX=6)` — angular size, not `devicePixelRatio`. No fractional path exists (a 2.5× bitmap font is just blurry).
- `geometry(w, h)` computes `PAD_L/R/T/B` from `MARGIN * UI` plus **safe-area insets** (`viewport-fit=cover` was putting the score behind the notch), `RIGHT/BOTTOM/CENTRE`, `CHARGE_W/H/Y`, `BANNER_Y`, `LIVE_Y`, `AIR_Y`. Read-outs hang from the top corners; the trick banner goes in the empty band *below* the corner blocks so it never lands on the rider.
- Palette is quantised to R5G5B5 by `q5(hex)` — `ICE #00d4ff`, `GOLD #ffab00`, `SNOW #e6eefa`, `QUIET`, `DIM`, `INK #060c16`. Never `#ffffff`.
- `clip(s, size, room)` truncates in one place, so no `draw` call site has a width check.
- Each string is drawn twice — glyphs, then the same glyphs one *display* pixel right, additive and faint — as a CRT phosphor-bleed.
- **Menus**: `drawBitmapMenu(g, isPaused)` paints `rgba(9,15,26,0.62)` over the frame (deliberately not opaque — the attract-mode rider must stay visible), a 2·UI ice `strokeRect`, `centreLine()`-ed items, a loading bar (`strokeRect` + `fillRect` × progress), and a blinking `[ PRESS ANY KEY TO DROP IN ]`. `LEGEND` (the control list) is **baked once into its own offscreen canvas** by `bakeLegend()` and blitted, invalidated only on a UI-scale change, shown for `LEGEND_SECONDS = 4`.
- **Redraw gating**: `signature(g)` builds a string of every value that could change a pixel (rounded score, combo, blink phases, speed, banner state, charge width…); `update(g, dt)` only calls `draw(g)` when the signature differs.
- Accessibility is first-class: `CALM = matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)')` — every flash has a still equivalent (colour instead of blink), and there's a visually hidden paragraph refreshed once a second (`speak`) plus an event-driven polite `[data-callout]` for banners, because a canvas gives a screen reader nothing.
- Public API: `{ update, banner, clearBanner, setMuted, resetScore, setSize, canvas }`. Discipline stated at the top: *the HUD only ever states what the physics already did.*

## 6. `audio.js` — procedural WebAudio

- **Zero audio files, by policy.** Everything is an oscillator or 2 seconds of noise generated at startup and filtered per job.
- Graph: `master (0.55) → DynamicsCompressor(threshold −10, knee 24, ratio 12, attack 3 ms, release 250 ms) → destination` — a soft limiter so a hard landing summing 8 voices doesn't clip.

  | voice | buffer | filter |
  |---|---|---|
  | `rush` (wind body, the only voice that survives a jump) | brown | lowpass 700, Q 0.7 |
  | `whistle` (only past ~half speed) | white | bandpass 1100, Q 2.6 |
  | `rumble` (board over ground) | brown | lowpass 160, Q 1.1 |
  | `edge` (carve, from `carveLoad`) | white | bandpass 2600, Q 3.4 |
  | `wash` (slide) | brown | bandpass 900, Q 0.8 |
  | `scrape` (fallen body, only on contact) | white | bandpass 1050, Q 0.95 |

Eight layers, all in one `Group` **moved to the rider every frame and never rotated** (parallax with nothing = distance). Nothing is baked; every colour is a uniform the weather writes per frame, so a full day cycle costs zero geometry work.

1. **Dome** — `SphereGeometry(2900, 96, 64)`, `BackSide`, custom `ShaderMaterial`, `depthWrite: false`, `renderOrder = 1` so it draws *after* the opaque terrain and early-z throws most of its fragments away. Three-stop gradient (`uZenith/uMid/uHorizon` + `uHaze`) plus a sun lobe (`pow(dot,7)*0.85 + pow(dot,2)*0.14`) — "the cheapest atmosphere in graphics". **The gradient's shape is duplicated verbatim in `shading.js` (`n64Sky`)** so a fogged ridge dissolves into the same sky standing behind it; both read the same uniforms so they can't drift.
2. **Panorama plates** — 4 equirectangular JPEGs (`alps-clear`, `alps-storm`, `alps-sunrise`, `alps-aurora-night`) sampled inside the dome shader, max contribution `PANO_MAX = 0.90`, `uPanoYaw = 0.25` puts the seam uphill. Careful async choreography: a 1×1 neutral `DataTexture` fallback, `settlePlates()` waits for *both* weather callbacks before binding (atomic sampler swap), and a late hour-plate only fills a variable — swapped in later through an out-of-sight dip in `panoWish/panoStage/panoReady`. Failing to load leaves a complete procedural sky.
3. **Counterglow / Earth-shadow belt** — a full ring (`SphereGeometry` band), which part shows is one dot product against the sun's flattened heading. **Alpha-blended, not additive** (the Earth's shadow is darker than the sky).
4. **Stars** — just inside the dome, faded in with night, first thing a storm removes.
5. **Aurora** — three octaves of scrolling noise in a vertical ramp, green foot/violet fringe, additive but deliberately quiet and cut high so most of the band is empty. `weather.aurora` gates it (~1 night in 4).
6. **Mist** — the only piece not at infinity. A **lattice of horizontal sheets** one every `MIST.spacing` metres of altitude, pinned to the world, 3 alive at a time (keyed on the *nearest* level, so a sheet only ever enters/leaves a level and a half away where its own fade has taken it). Alpha is the honest integral: depth ÷ sin(view angle), so a bank at eye height fills the frame and the same bank underfoot is a floor you can see through. Per-level density from a noise field indexed by level number → valleys that have filled to a line. Fades out along the fog ramp and *in* over the first ~90 m (else you can't steer).
7. **Haze cone** — `MeshBasicMaterial` cone of exactly the fog colour under everything, hiding the mesh's edge. Its **pitch is measured, not assumed**: two probes into `heightAt` at `RENDER.fogFar` and `TERRAIN.ahead`, taken on `nearestCenter` (not the rider's x), the steeper wins, eased at `PITCH_EASE = 0.5`/s and clamped to `[PITCH_MIN, PITCH_MAX]` derived from the terrain grade waves.
8. **Background mountains — two systems:**

Parallax fraction is derived, not tuned: a ring at radius R that must read as D away moves by `R/D` of the camera's translation — and that debt is paid **around the circumference** rather than as a translation, so an endless run never has to wrap. Only the (bounded) lateral component is paid honestly. Profile is a *product*, not a sum: massifs (5 around the ring) multiplied into ridged horns (18) multiplied by knife edges (48), `sharp 1.8`, `floor 0.22` — cols with nothing in them, corners at the summits. Snow line is a threshold on the height varying that was already there (`above 0.88`, `wobble 0.12`, `glacier 0.36` — glaciers drawn by *moving the snow line down*, not painting on top; rock goes *above* the snow line where the skyline falls fastest). Per-band air `airAt(far) = 1 - exp(-far/12000)` drives sky bleed (`SKY_BLEED 0.62`), contrast survival and relief flattening — one exponential keeps four bands in agreement.

Long, empirically-verified comment at sky.js:2277 about `normalBias` doing nothing to the terrain (no `normal` attribute → `HAS_NORMAL` compiled out) — worth reading before copying shadow settings.

**Weather** (`weather.js`) is four continuous dials, none of them a preset name: `tod` (full day in 3 min, interpolated through **9 moments** each carrying the whole picture — including FIRST LIGHT and BLUE HOUR where the sun is allowed *under* the horizon), `storm` (drifting slow noise; pulls colours to haze, fog from 400 m to 70 m, halves the light, thickens snowfall), `mist` (cold-air: driven by `(1-sunElevation)·(1-moon)` and a *hump* in storm), and wind. `sky.update(pos, w, dt)`; `sky.project(camera)` is separate because the crepuscular pass needs the sun's screen position after the chase camera has settled.

## 4. `shading.js` — the shared material patch

`createShading(THREE)` returns `{ apply, update, reset, ... }`. Every material in the game (terrain, props, trail, rider, huts, wildlife, helicopter) goes through `apply` — there is no unpatched path on purpose.

**`apply(material, opts)`** installs an `onBeforeCompile` and:
- **calls any pre-existing `onBeforeCompile` first** and keeps its edits (this is the contract props.js/terrain.js lean on);
- `Object.assign(shader.uniforms, uniforms, own)` — **shared uniform objects by reference**, so one write per frame in `update()` moves fog/sky/sun across six modules that know nothing about each other;
- patches vertex: `common` → `VERT_PARS` (`varying vec3 vN64View; varying float vN64Ice, vN64Sheen;`), `project_vertex` → keeps `mvPosition.xyz` (geometry is never snapped — the old vertex-snap/light-banding retro treatment was retired);
- patches fragment at four anchors, each guarded by an `indexOf` check so unlit materials silently skip:
  - `lights_fragment_maps` → **`FRAG_SHADE`**: the mountain's own horizon shadow, a *world-aligned toroidal* atlas (5×5 tiles, 480 m modulo) marched by terrain.js — so a tree at the foot of the containment wall is shadowed by the wall even though the depth map doesn't hold the mountain;
  - `lights_fragment_end` → **`lightPatch(sheen)`** = `FRAG_SUN` + `FRAG_RECOVER` + `FRAG_SHEEN`. `FRAG_RECOVER` **divides the shadow back out of `directDiffuse`** (`albedo·dotNL·sunRadiance·shadow/π`, everything but shadow is in scope) instead of doing a second PCF lookup. `FRAG_SHEEN` is a GGX microfacet snow response — `SHEEN.f0 = 0.018` (real ice), roughness from a snowpack field (`vN64Ice`), Schlick Fresnel to reflected sky at grazing angles, and a wrapped subsurface term. Gated by a luminance mask (`SNOW_LO 0.22 / SNOW_HI 0.42`) times `uSheen` times per-vertex `vN64Sheen`, so rock and everything that never asked skip the expensive second sky evaluation;
  - `fog_fragment` → **`FRAG_FOG`**: three's fog is disabled (`material.fog = false`) and replaced by directional aerial perspective — `mix(colour, n64Sky(viewDir), smoothstep(fogNear, fogFar, dist * uFogPull))` plus a height-based valley-mist term that blends to the flat haze stop (never the directional gradient — routing it through the sun lobe turned golden-hour slopes mud-brown). Branch-skipped when `fog < 0.003`;
  - `alphamap_fragment` → **`FRAG_CAMERA_FADE`**: `diffuseColor.a *= smoothstep(2.2, 6.5, length(vN64View))` + `material.alphaHash = true`, so the chase camera inside a conifer screen-doors it away without sorting errors.
- **`uFogPull`** is the notable per-material knob: how much *further away* a surface pretends to be when asking the curtain. Snow is already haze-coloured and vanishes at f≈0.5; a dark crown needs f≈0.95 — without this the ground dissolves out from under a forest that doesn't. Props pass `FOG_PULL_TREE/STONE/FLORA`.
- **`customProgramCacheKey`** is mandatory here and explained: three's default key is the *text* of `onBeforeCompile`, and every patched material shares one closure with identical text, so without a key the terrain and the trees would collide on one program. The key encodes the patches requested plus `prev.toString()`.
- `SKY_GLSL` is exported and included by **both** the dome material and every lit material's fog term — the cloud deck is a ray/plane intersection (4 instructions) sampled in a wrapping 64-cell procedural noise field, written to keep operands `mediump`-honest. A separate `n64SkyReflect` is the same sky *without* the cloud octaves, for the rough snow reflection.
- `createCloudShadowTexture` bakes 3 periodic value-noise octaves into a 128×128 `RedFormat` DataTexture (16 KiB) — one filtered read per fragment gives every material the same cloud shadow.

Other `onBeforeCompile` patches in props.js: `treeMat` / `floraMat` / `rockMat` add **triplanar textures** in `color_fragment` (bark ×3 axes weighted by `abs(normal)`, needles by world xz, `step(0.35, diffuseColor.g)` picks bark vs needle), `alpineMat` maps wood planks, `lampMat`/`pisteStakeLampMat` are unlit `MeshBasicMaterial` with `toneMapped = false` whose `color_vertex` is replaced by `BEACON`/`PISTE_BEACON` — a flash that is a pure function of `uAirTime`, phase from `instanceMatrix[3].z` (so both poles of a gate flash together and consecutive gates ripple), and `uNextGate` promotes the leader with a faster clock and 2× output. Lamps keep three's fog so a beacon still dies in a whiteout.

## 5. `hud.js` + `font.js` — the retro 5×7 bitmap read-out

### `font.js` (276 lines)
- Each glyph is **5 columns × 7 bits**, bit 0 = top row (the HD44780 convention). `GLYPH_W 5, GLYPH_H 7, ADVANCE 6, LINE 9`. Monospace on purpose — tabular figures by not having any other kind.
- `GLYPHS` is a flat `{char: [5 bytes]}` table: A–Z, 0–9, and exactly the punctuation the HUD speaks (`. , : · + × — - ° / % ( ) [ ] < > ◀ ▶ ▲ ▼ ✦ ← Ⅱ ♪`). Missing glyphs draw `TOFU` (a hollow box), never a space.
- **Halo/outline**: derived by bit dilation, not by drawing 8 times. `smeared[i] = c | c<<1 | c>>1` (vertical), then each halo column ORs its two neighbours (horizontal) → a 7×9 bitmap, cached in `halos: Map`. Because advance (6) > ink (5), a halo occupies the air column and never touches a neighbour's ink — which is what makes one-pass-per-string safe.
- **Sprite cache**: each `(char, size, colour, halo)` is baked once into its own offscreen canvas (halo pass then ink pass) and every subsequent appearance is one `drawImage` at integer coords and native scale. `column()` emits vertical *runs* as `fillRect`s (≈8 rects/glyph instead of 35). `SPRITE_LIMIT = 384`, cleared wholesale when full.
- API: `drawText(ctx, str, x, y, colour, size = 1, halo = null)` (upper-cases on the way in, skips spaces, returns the width) and `measure(str, size)` (doesn't count the trailing air column).

### `hud.js` (910 lines)
- A **second canvas** (`.readout`, `aria-hidden`) sized to the *display*, not the adaptive 3D target, so text stays sharp when the GPU lowers world resolution. `ctx.imageSmoothingEnabled = false`; everything lands on whole buffer pixels.
- **Scale in whole stops only**: `UI = min(round(H / LINES_PER_STOP=400), floor(min(W/FOOT_W, H/FOOT_H)), UI_MAX=6)` — angular size, not `devicePixelRatio`. No fractional path exists (a 2.5× bitmap font is just blurry).
- `geometry(w, h)` computes `PAD_L/R/T/B` from `MARGIN * UI` plus **safe-area insets** (`viewport-fit=cover` was putting the score behind the notch), `RIGHT/BOTTOM/CENTRE`, `CHARGE_W/H/Y`, `BANNER_Y`, `LIVE_Y`, `AIR_Y`. Read-outs hang from the top corners; the trick banner goes in the empty band *below* the corner blocks so it never lands on the rider.
- Palette is quantised to R5G5B5 by `q5(hex)` — `ICE #00d4ff`, `GOLD #ffab00`, `SNOW #e6eefa`, `QUIET`, `DIM`, `INK #060c16`. Never `#ffffff`.
- `clip(s, size, room)` truncates in one place, so no `draw` call site has a width check.
- Each string is drawn twice — glyphs, then the same glyphs one *display* pixel right, additive and faint — as a CRT phosphor-bleed.
- **Menus**: `drawBitmapMenu(g, isPaused)` paints `rgba(9,15,26,0.62)` over the frame (deliberately not opaque — the attract-mode rider must stay visible), a 2·UI ice `strokeRect`, `centreLine()`-ed items, a loading bar (`strokeRect` + `fillRect` × progress), and a blinking `[ PRESS ANY KEY TO DROP IN ]`. `LEGEND` (the control list) is **baked once into its own offscreen canvas** by `bakeLegend()` and blitted, invalidated only on a UI-scale change, shown for `LEGEND_SECONDS = 4`.
- **Redraw gating**: `signature(g)` builds a string of every value that could change a pixel (rounded score, combo, blink phases, speed, banner state, charge width…); `update(g, dt)` only calls `draw(g)` when the signature differs.
- Accessibility is first-class: `CALM = matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)')` — every flash has a still equivalent (colour instead of blink), and there's a visually hidden paragraph refreshed once a second (`speak`) plus an event-driven polite `[data-callout]` for banners, because a canvas gives a screen reader nothing.
- Public API: `{ update, banner, clearBanner, setMuted, resetScore, setSize, canvas }`. Discipline stated at the top: *the HUD only ever states what the physics already did.*

---

## 6. `audio.js` — procedural WebAudio

- **Zero audio files, by policy.** Everything is an oscillator or 2 seconds of noise generated at startup and filtered per job.
- Graph: `master (0.55) → DynamicsCompressor(threshold −10, knee 24, ratio 12, attack 3 ms, release 250 ms) → destination` — a soft limiter so a hard landing summing 8 voices doesn't clip.
- **Two noise buffers**: brown (white through a leaky integrator, `last = (last + 0.024*n)/1.024`) for wind and board rumble; white for hisses, because a resonant filter has nothing to find above 6 dB/octave rolloff.
- **Six continuous voices**, each `BufferSource(loop) → BiquadFilter → Gain → master`, gains driven straight from the physics in `ambience(speed, slide, grounded, storm, carveLoad, tumbleSlide, surf)`:
  | voice | buffer | filter |
  |---|---|---|
  | `rush` (wind body, the only voice that survives a jump) | brown | lowpass 700, Q 0.7 |
  | `whistle` (only past ~half speed) | white | bandpass 1100, Q 2.6 |
  | `rumble` (board over ground) | brown | lowpass 160, Q 1.1 |
  | `edge` (carve, from `carveLoad`) | white | bandpass 2600, Q 3.4 |
  | `wash` (slide) | brown | bandpass 900, Q 0.8 |
  | `scrape` (fallen body, only on contact) | white | bandpass 1050, Q 0.95 |
  All snow voices go to zero in the air — "a jump is quiet and the landing is loud" is the whole design.
- **Two one-shot primitives**: `tone(freq, endFreq, dur, gain, type, delay)` (oscillator + exponential frequency ramp + attack/decay envelope) and `burst(dur, freq, gain, filterType, sweepTo, delay, buffer)` (noise source with randomised `playbackRate` 0.85–1.15 and a random start offset into the buffer, so repeated landings aren't the identical grain).
- Events built from those: `jump, chime, stomp, land, trick, combo, crash, bodyImpact, push, whoosh, thud`.
- Lifecycle care: `start()` runs on **every** resume (not just the first) because browsers suspend the context in a background tab; `parked` tracks *intent* separately from the async `ctx.state`; `toggleMute` ramps rather than steps (a gain step under six voices is an audible click); `ambience` is not gated on mute so the gains keep tracking the run.

## 7. Assets: provenance and loading pattern

### `assets/textures/GENERATED.md`
States plainly: **"Generated with built-in image-generation tools for real-time WebGL use."** No download, no third-party licence, no attribution requirement. It is a catalogue in 5 groups with a one-line prompt-style description each: terrain/snowpack (`snow/powder-surface.webp`, `snow/groomed-surface.webp`, `snow/ice-glacier.jpg`, `rock/rock-granite.jpg`, `rock/rock-sandstone.jpg`, `rock/rock-slate.jpg`), player/NPC (`rider/snowboard-graphics.jpg`, `rider/snowboard-retro.jpg`, `rider/rider-fabric.jpg`), huts (`huts/alpine-wood-planks.jpg`, `huts/shingle-roof-snow.jpg`), trees (`tree/pine-needles.jpg`, `tree/frosty-conifer-boughs.jpg`, `tree/tree-bark.jpg`, `tree/weathered-tree-bark.jpg`), sky panoramas (`sky/alps-clear.webp`, `alps-storm.webp`, `alps-sunrise.jpg`, `alps-aurora-night.jpg`, `alps-peaks-sunset.jpg`). ~20 MB total on disk.

### `assets/models/MODELS.md`
**Downloaded**, with full provenance: Quaternius low-poly nature set (winter variants), **CC0 / public domain**, from quaternius.com, obtained 2026-08-07 via the MIT-licensed mirror `github.com/flo-bit/tiny-planets` (`public/lowpoly_nature/`). glTF 2.0 with embedded buffers, exported by FBX2glTF. 20 files, 1.8 MB (`PineTree_Snow_1-5`, `CommonTree_Snow_1-3`, `CommonTree_Dead_Snow_1-2`, `BirchTree_Dead_Snow_1`, `Rock_Snow_1-7`, `TreeStump_Snow`, `WoodLog_Snow`). Vendored loaders (`assets/vendor/GLTFLoader.js`, `assets/utils/BufferGeometryUtils.js`, `assets/utils/SkeletonUtils.js`) are three.js r185, MIT, matching the vendored three build at the repo root.

### Texture loading pattern (consistent across the codebase)
```js
const neutral = new THREE.DataTexture(new Uint8Array([128,128,128,255]), 1, 1, THREE.RGBAFormat);
neutral.needsUpdate = true;
const barkTex = { value: neutral };                     // the uniform object itself
texLoader.load(
  new URL('../assets/textures/tree/weathered-tree-bark.jpg', import.meta.url).href,
  (t) => { t.wrapS = t.wrapT = THREE.RepeatWrapping; barkTex.value = t; },
);
```
Key points to copy:
- The **uniform record is created up front holding a 1×1 neutral `DataTexture`** and handed to every material by reference; the load callback mutates `.value`. Nothing waits, nothing recompiles, and a 404 leaves a fully playable procedural fallback.
- Paths are always `new URL('../assets/...', import.meta.url).href` — module-relative, works from any mount point.
- `terrain.js` adds a settle-not-reject promise wrapper (`loadSurface`/`loadRock` → `Promise.all` → `surfacesReady`) so a loading bar can report progress without hanging forever on a failed fetch, plus `prepareSurface()` (RepeatWrapping, mipmaps, `NoColorSpace`, `anisotropy = maxAnisotropy`).
- `sky.js` uses `preparePlate()` (RepeatWrapping S / ClampToEdge T, LinearFilter, `generateMipmaps: false`, `SRGBColorSpace`) and the atomic two-callback `settlePlates()` gate described in §3.
- Models: `createModelUpgrader(THREE)` (`importedModels.js`) loads asynchronously *after* the pools exist and **hot-swaps `pool.mesh.geometry`** — instance matrices, casts, sway and shadow bookkeeping all reference the mesh, not the geometry, so nothing else knows. `bakePoolGeometry` merges the glTF scene into one non-indexed geometry emitting the exact same attribute contract the growers do (position/normal/colour-as-value/`surfaceOwn`): owned surfaces → greys via `valueOf(lum)` (`V_LO 0.55`, `V_SPAN 0.50`), snow keeps near-white with `surfaceOwn = 0`, rocks bake straight into the terrain's slate/iron palette by luminance. `normalise()` grounds and uniformly scales to the height the material was compiled for, with a `sink` fraction below grade. On error: *"the grown variant simply remains."* Only pines and dead trees are used — broadleaf variants "read as summer trees wearing snow and break the biome."

### Two loose ends worth knowing before you copy
- `sky.js` loads `alps-clear.jpg` / `alps-storm.jpg`; GENERATED.md documents those two as `.webp`. Both formats exist on disk, so the `.webp` pair is unused.
- Unreferenced in code: `rock/rock-sandstone.jpg`, `rider/snowboard-retro.jpg`, `snow/ice-glacier.jpg`, `tree/pine-needles.jpg`, `tree/tree-bark.jpg`, `sky/alps-peaks-sunset.jpg`, and the two `.webp` skies — roughly a third of the texture payload ships unused.</result>

1	/* The mountain.
2	
3	   There is no terrain data. `heightAt` is a pure function of a coordinate and
4	   everything else in the game reads the hill through it: the rider stands on
5	   it, ramps are built on top of it, trees are planted on it, and the mesh
6	   below is only ever a picture of it.
7	
8	   Four things have changed about what that function says, and they are the
9	   whole of the mountain's character.
10	
11	   The pitch is no longer constant. It is two long sines over a base, and the
12	   height is their analytic integral — which matters more than it sounds,
13	   because the alternative is marching down the hill from the summit every
14	   time anything asks how high the ground is, five times per physics step. So
15	   the run has chapters: pitches that stand up and ask for a real carve, and
16	   runouts that hand the speed back slowly.
17	
18	   The route forks. Every few hundred metres the single centre line has a
19	   chance of splitting in two, drifting apart around an island and closing
20	   again below. The corridor is measured to whichever branch is nearer, so
21	   the geometry does the rest by itself: the piste widens, an island of hill
22	   rises out of the middle of it, two lines run either side, and they rejoin.
23	
24	   The corridor is roughly three times wider than it was, and it breathes —
25	   gullies where it draws in, bowls where it opens out.
26	
27	   And you cannot leave it. Outside the groomed part the ground rises into a
28	   quarterpipe with a real lip you can launch off, and past that into a wall
29	   that climbs towards a hundred and thirty metres and then keeps creeping up
30	   forever. Crossing it takes about 75 m/s of kinetic energy; high flow can
31	   now clear it, while ordinary runs remain contained. There is no barrier or
32	   invisible wall — the ground outside the run is simply, monotonically,
33	   uphill everywhere, so gravity is always pointing home.
34	
35	   The mesh is a single graded grid, re-anchored to the rider in whole cells
36	   and refilled from `heightAt`. Snapping to whole cells is what keeps the
37	   facets welded to the ground instead of crawling across it; grading the
38	   cells is what lets six thousand vertices cover most of a kilometre. */
39	
40	import { snoise2, noise2, hash2, getWorldSeed } from './noise.js';
41	import { TERRAIN, RENDER } from './config.js';
42	import { buildShadowRegion } from './shadow-cache.js';
43	
44	/* THE SNOWPACK — what the ground is made of, as against how it is lit.
45	
46	   The hill's shape was already a function of where you are on it and its
47	   surface was not. Every flat was the same snow and every steep face was the
48	   same rock, which is a mountain built out of one material and then bent, and
49	   the eye reads that immediately even when it cannot say why: two kilometres
50	   of descent went past and nothing about the ground had changed.
51	
52	   So the cover is now a small budget that four things spend, and rock is
53	   simply what is left where the budget runs out.
54	
55	   ALTITUDE is the strongest of them and it is the one a real mountain wears
56	   most plainly. The run loses about 0.28 metres of height per metre of z, so
57	   a kilometre of riding is nearly three hundred metres of descent, and three
58	   hundred metres is the difference between ground the wind has scoured to ice
59	   and ground that has held everything that fell on it since November. It is
60	   `ctx.base` — the grade's own integral, which is metres below the summit and
61	   already computed once a row — and so it costs a subtraction.
62	
63	   It saturates, and that is not a fudge. The run is endless: taken literally,
64	   an absolute snow line is crossed once in the first four kilometres and then
65	   the mountain is one material for ever, which is the bug this is meant to
66	   fix. What actually happens on a mountain is that below the scour zone the
67	   pack stops deepening with height and starts varying with everything else,
68	   and below the snow line proper there is no snow at all — which this run
69	   cannot have, because it is a snowboard game. So the altitude term does its
70	   work over the first kilometre and a half of descent and then hands over.
71	
72	   RELIEF is what it hands over to, and it is permanent because it is local:
73	   `h - ctx.base` is how far this vertex stands above the plane the grade says
74	   the run should be on. Inside the corridor that is the ridge and roll
75	   octaves, so the broad swells get their crests scoured and their hollows
76	   filled — wind scour and lee drift, from a subtraction that was already
77	   free. Outside it, it is the lip and then the containment wall, which climb
78	   sixty metres and more, and which therefore become the scoured rock ribs of
79	   a valley rather than two white banks standing beside the piste. The run
80	   reads as a trough on a mountain, which is what it is.
81	
82	   ASPECT. A slope that faces the sun keeps less snow than one that does not,
83	   and this is measured against a fixed bearing rather than against the live
84	   sun. That was the second attempt. The first read `shading.uniforms.uSunDir`
85	   at fill time, which is wrong twice over: snow depth is a season and not a
86	   moment, so a slope does not grow rock at noon and lose it at four; and the
87	   vertex colours are only rebuilt when the mesh re-anchors, so a rider who
88	   stopped would have watched the mountain change material underneath them one
89	   LOD ring at a time. The bearing here is the mean of the azimuth swing in
90	   `weather.js` — where the sun spends its day — and it is a constant.
91	
92	   BANDS. A slow noise along the run, sheared so that its edges run diagonally
93	   across the hill instead of squarely across it, saying that this stretch is
94	   a rock band and that one is a snowfield. The grade already gives the run
95	   chapters; this gives the same stretches a material.
96	
97	   And the corridor is exempted from most of it, because a piste is groomed.
98	   Machines put that snow there and keep it there, which is exactly why a real
99	   high alpine piste is a white ribbon laid over bare rock — and it is also
100	   what keeps the run legible when the mountain around it has gone to stone.
101	
102	   THE COLOUR. Three snow stops, and the axis between them is not brightness,
103	   it is what the snow has been through. Deep soft cover is the palest and the

302	/* The mid-line: where the run would be if it never split. */
303	export function wanderAt(z) {
304	  let x = 0;

309	/* Half the separation between the two branches, and zero wherever the run is
310	   whole. A fork gets one window per `period` metres of hill, takes it about
311	   two thirds of the time, and opens and closes over the first and last third
312	   of the window it occupies — so from inside, a fork is a piste that widens,
313	   grows an island, and closes again. */

316	  if (b < 0) return 0;

318	  const top = -(b * route.period) - (route.period - route.span) * hash2(b, 991, 42);

355	/* ==========================================================================
356	   The guide — the racing line, and the groomed ribbon that follows it.
357	
358	   Gates stand on a fixed rhythm down the mountain: one per `guide.every`
359	   metres, jittered inside its own slot, everything about it hashed off the
360	   slot index alone so a gate stands in the same place however the terrain
361	   around it is rebuilt, restarted or re-entered. The guide line is the
362	   smooth curve through those gates — flat through each gate, swinging
363	   between them — and the groomer drives exactly that line: glass corduroy

370	function gateSlotZ(k) {
371	  // 0.25..0.75 into the slot: adjacent gates can never stand closer than

373	  return -(k + 0.25 + 0.50 * hash2(k, 61, 47)) * guide.every;

379	   itself opens and closes smoothly and the side holds while it does. */

381	  const s = forkSplit(z);

390	  const drift = Math.min(16, Math.max(0, corridorHalfAt(z) - guide.margin));

398	/* The line itself, at any z. The course centre is evaluated *here*, not at

export const TERRAIN = {
     A constant grade is a ramp, and a ramp has one idea in it. This is two
     sines over a base, so the run has chapters: a pitch that stands up and
     asks for a real carve, a runout that gives the speed back slowly, and
     the transitions between them where the ground quietly stops falling
     away and the rider has to work for the first time in a kilometre.
     It stays a closed form because `heightAt` has to. The height is the
     integral of this, done analytically in `terrain.js` — sampling a varying
     grade would mean marching from the top of the mountain every time the
     rider asked how high the ground was, five times per physics step. Both
     amplitudes are held well under the base so the sum never reaches zero:
     the hill is allowed to get lazy and is never allowed to point back up. */
  grade: {
    base: 0.30,       // 16.7° — the low end of a real red run
    waves: [
      { freq: 0.00085, amp: 0.050, phase: 0 },      // ~7.4 km, the big chapters
      { freq: 0.00310, amp: 0.035, phase: 2.1 },    // ~2.0 km, pitches inside them
         rider has to check speed on, a mellow shelf to catch a breath and
         pump for the next one — the difference between a treadmill and a
         mountain. Kept small enough that the combined trough stays near 10°,
         which the slope budget below still survives. */
      { freq: 0.00900, amp: 0.040, phase: 4.4 },
    ],
  },
     steepest — and the shallow end of that is the number every other term on
     this mountain has to be budgeted against. See `SLOPE BUDGET` below.
     Both amplitudes came down by a third when that budget was worked out.
     They were ±0.177, which put the gentlest chapters at 6.9°, and 6.9° is
     shallower than the rolling ground's own faces — so those stretches
     genuinely pointed uphill in places and a rider who arrived slowly simply
     stopped on them, which is not a difficulty curve, it is a bug. */
     the run arrives somewhere rather than pointing at the same spot forever,
     and a bend gives the rider a reason to carve that the terrain alone
     never would.
     THE LATERAL RATE IS Σ(amp·freq), and it is a budget for the same reason
     the fall-line one is — it was simply never written down, so nothing kept
     it honest. The line under this table used to claim the route drifts about
     seven metres sideways for every hundred it descends; the three sines
     actually summed to thirteen, because a claim about "both amplitudes"
     being small against "their wavelengths" is a statement about each of them
     separately and the rider only ever meets the sum. At thirteen per cent
     the corridor slides sideways at four metres a second under a rider doing
     thirty, which is most of a piste width every ten seconds and is felt as
     the run walking out from under you.
     The shortest wave is where nearly all of it was: at a wavelength of 1570
     metres it carried half the total rate on a fifth of the amplitude. Pulled
     back to eleven it costs the route almost none of its shape, and the two
     long ones — which are the ones that make the run arrive somewhere — are
     untouched. */
  wander: [
    { freq: 0.0040, amp: 11 },
    { freq: 0.0013, amp: 34 },
    { freq: 0.00047, amp: 52 },   // the long one: whole shoulders of mountain
  ],
     Every `period` metres the mountain gets the chance to open a fork, and
     when it takes one the single centre line becomes two, drifting apart to
     `split` either side over the first third of the window, holding, and
     closing again. The corridor is measured to the *nearer* of the two, so
     what happens on the ground is exactly what happens on a real mountain:
     the piste widens, an island of trees rises out of the middle of it, the
     two lines run either side of the island, and they rejoin below.
     `split` has to beat the corridor's half-width for an island to exist at
     all — below that the two corridors simply overlap and the run is briefly
     twice as wide, which is a perfectly good thing for it to be and is what
     the opening and closing of every fork looks like from inside. */
  route: {
    period: 520,
    chance: 0.80,
    span: 300,        // metres the fork stays open
    split: 72,        // half-separation at full opening
       A fork where both ways are level is a choice with no content — the
       lines are mirror images and it does not matter which you take. Give one
       of them ten metres of elevation over the other and it becomes a real
       decision: the high line is slower to reach and pays it back as speed
       down the far side, the low line is quicker now and arrives flat. The
       offset is blended by inverse-square proximity to each branch rather
       than switched at the midpoint, so the island between them sits at the
       mean and there is no seam anywhere on the hill. */
    drop: 11,

/* Sommer's numbers, in one place. The layout follows Alpen's config: every
   value here is read by name from the modules, and the comments say what a
   number *does*, not what it is. Downhill is −z everywhere. */

export const RENDER = {
  fov: 68,
  fovAtSpeed: 78,      // reached as speed approaches RIDER.maxSpeed
  near: 0.1,
  far: 2600,
  fogNear: 180,
  fogFar: 620,
  fogColor: '#dcebf7', // the horizon haze — the dome hands over to this
  maxPixelRatio: 1.75,
};

export const TERRAIN = {
  /* The pitch: a base grade with two long sines over it, integrated
     analytically in terrain.js. Gentler than a ski run — a bike trail loses
     about 13% and breathes between steep pitches and near-flat runouts. */
  grade: {
    base: 0.24,
    waves: [
      { freq: 0.0009, amp: 0.050, phase: 0 },     // the big chapters
      { freq: 0.0034, amp: 0.045, phase: 2.1 },   // pitches inside them
      { freq: 0.0110, amp: 0.045, phase: 4.4 },   // rollers you feel
    ],
  },

  /* The trail's mid-line drift. Σ(amp·freq) ≈ 0.10 — the corridor slides
     sideways a metre for every ten ridden, which reads as a mountain trail
     finding its way rather than a slalom. */
  wander: [
    { freq: 0.0052, amp: 8 },
    { freq: 0.0016, amp: 30 },
    { freq: 0.00052, amp: 48 },
  ],

  /* The singletrack itself: a narrow carved bed with soft shoulders. `bed`
     is the smooth rideable half-width, `shoulder` the rough verge it fades
     across, and `swing` extra bed jitter so the line snakes inside the
     corridor. */
  trail: {
    bed: 2.3,
    shoulder: 2.8,
    swing: { freq: 0.021, amp: 2.6 },
    /* Berms: the bed banks into turns. The tilt is the guide line's own
       curvature times this, clamped — outside edge up, like a dug berm. */
    bermGain: 34,
    bermMax: 0.55,     // max lateral slope of the bed (~29°)
    crown: 0.18,       // the bed stands a hand above the meadow it crosses
  },

  /* The wider corridor of open, rideable-if-rough ground either side of the
     bed before the valley stands up. */
  corridor: { half: 22, vary: 7, freq: 0.0013, bowl: 2.6 },

  /* Beyond the corridor: a shoulder rise, then flanks that climb forever —
     gravity always points home. Softer and greener than Alpen's walls. */
  valley: {
    rise: 7,          // over the shoulder band
    band: 26,         // metres of rough shoulder before the flank
    height: 90,       // the flank's exponential saturation height
    scale: 130,       // its lateral scale
    creep: 0.16,      // and the forever-upward creep past it
    creepEase: 40,
  },

  /* The open-ground octaves. Damped to nothing on the trail bed; full
     strength in the meadows and woods. Amplitudes are per-zone-scaled in
     terrain.js. */
  ridges: { freq: 0.0034, amp: 3.2, seed: 5 },
  rolls: { freq: 0.010, amp: 1.5, seed: 1 },
  bumps: { freq: 0.055, amp: 0.30, seed: 2 },
  chatter: { freq: 0.30, amp: 0.045, seed: 3 },
  warp: { freq: 0.0042, amp: 24, seed: 8 },

  /* The zones — what the brief calls the terrain kinds. Two slow dials and
     a hashed window system derive five blended weights in terrain.js:
     pine forest, mixed forest, meadow, rocky ridge, bike park. */
  zones: {
    forestFreq: 0.0011,  // wooded ↔ open
    stoneFreq: 0.00072,  // soft ground ↔ rocky ridge
    mixFreq: 0.0035,     // pine ↔ mixed, inside the woods
    seed: 21,
    /* Bike-park windows: every `period` m of hill, `chance` of a park
       `span` m long. Parks only open where the ridge dial is low. */
    park: { period: 1100, chance: 0.6, span: 260 },
    /* Rocky exposure: in ridge zones one side of the trail falls away.
       `drop` metres over `reach` m laterally, then the flank climbs back. */
    exposure: { drop: 22, reach: 34 },
  },

  /* Park furniture, carved into the bed itself: rollers and kickers as
     analytic bumps along the guide line. */
  park: {
    rollerWave: 26,    // metres between rollers
    rollerAmp: 0.55,
    kickerEvery: 78,   // a proper lip every so often
    kickerHeight: 1.5,
    kickerLength: 9,
  },

  /* The mesh: one graded grid re-anchored to the rider in whole cells. */
  spacing: 0.8,
  uniformNear: 56,
  ahead: 640,
  aheadGrowth: 1.06,
  side: 420,
  sideGrowth: 1.07,
  behind: 220,
  behindGrowth: 1.13,
};

export const RIDER = {
  gravity: 20,          // deliberately brisk, like Alpen's 22
  eyeHeight: 1.58,

  /* Steering: yaw authority falls with speed, grip caps lateral force. */
  steerRate: 2.6,       // rad/s at walking pace
  steerAtSpeed: 0.34,   // fraction of it left at maxSpeed
  grip: 11,             // m/s² of lateral hold on a perfect surface
  driftSlip: 0.86,      // how much of the spilled demand becomes slide
  selfCentre: 3.0,      // slip-angle self-straightening (board-frame!)

  /* Speeds. Pedalling is a floor that rises, not a force. */
  maxSpeed: 26,         // m/s ≈ 94 km/h terminal on a steep chapter
  pedalAccel: 5.0,
  pedalCap: 12.5,       // legs alone on the flat
  friction: 0.012,      // rolling
  drag: 0.0045,
  brakeFriction: 0.55,
  brakeEngage: 10,
  brakeRelease: 14,

  /* Bunny-hop: held to preload, released to pop. */
  chargeTime: 0.4,
  popMin: 2.1,
  popMax: 4.6,
  lipBonus: 1.35,       // released right on a lip
  airSteer: 2.2,        // m/s² of lateral drift authority in the air
  airPitch: 3.0,        // visual pitch control

  /* Launch look-ahead sweep (Alpen's predictor, shorter horizon). */
  launchHorizon: 0.08,
  launchGap: 0.10,
  launchSampleSpacing: 0.30,
  launchSampleMax: 96,

  /* Landing and crashing. */
  softImpact: 7,
  hardImpact: 15,       // beyond this the front washes out
  fallMin: 0.8,
  fallMax: 3.2,
  fallRest: 2.4,
  riseTime: 0.6,
  graceAfterRise: 1.4,

  /* Obstacle strikes. */
  brushSpeed: 5,
  wipeoutSpeed: 12,

  /* Suspension — one damped spring driving fork dip and eye bob. */
  springFreq: 2.9,
  springDamp: 0.72,
  compressPerG: 0.13,
  compressMax: 0.5,
};

export const CAMERA = {
  lookAhead: 10,
  headLag: 9,         // how quickly the head settles onto the travel line
  rollShare: 0.55,    // of the bike's lean shown as horizon roll
  bobAmp: 0.035,
  shake: 0.5,
  landPunch: 6,       // deg of FOV, decaying
  landPunchDecay: 4.0,
};

export const PROPS = {
  band: 40,
  ahead: 10,
  behind: 3,
  treesPerBand: 42,
  bushesPerBand: 26,
  rocksPerBand: 10,
  tuftsPerBand: 70,
  flowersPerBand: 40,
  verge: 1.6,         // nothing stands within bed + shoulder + this
};

};

   letter is made of exactly the same square pixels as the snow behind it.
   That single constraint rules out every real typeface: a font renderer
   would give back grey edges, and one grey pixel next to a hard-edged
   mountain is the whole illusion gone. A console of that era did not have a
   font renderer; it had a page of glyphs someone drew on graph paper and
   blitted. So does this.

  '<': [0x08, 0x14, 0x22, 0x41, 0x00],
  '>': [0x00, 0x41, 0x22, 0x14, 0x08],
  '◀': [0x08, 0x1c, 0x3e, 0x7f, 0x00],
  '▶': [0x00, 0x7f, 0x3e, 0x1c, 0x08],
  '▲': [0x20, 0x30, 0x38, 0x30, 0x20],
  '▼': [0x04, 0x0c, 0x1c, 0x0c, 0x04],
  '✦': [0x08, 0x1c, 0x77, 0x1c, 0x08],
  '←': [0x08, 0x1c, 0x2a, 0x08, 0x08],
  'Ⅱ': [0x00, 0x7f, 0x00, 0x7f, 0x00],
  '♪': [0x60, 0x50, 0x4f, 0x00, 0x00],
};

/* Anything not in the table draws as a hollow box, which is the honest
   answer: a missing glyph should look missing rather than look like a
   space, because a space is a thing the layout might legitimately want. */
const TOFU = [0x7f, 0x41, 0x41, 0x41, 0x7f];

/* The dilation described in the header. The glyph's rows 0-6 land on the
   halo's rows 1-7, which is what the `<< 1` is; rows 0 and 8 of the halo can
   only ever be lit by the vertical smear, which is exactly right. */
const halos = new Map();

function haloFor(ch) {
  let h = halos.get(ch);
  if (h) return h;
  const g = GLYPHS[ch] || TOFU;
  const smeared = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0];
  for (let i = 0; i < GLYPH_W; i++) {
    const c = g[i] << 1;
    smeared[i] = c | (c << 1) | (c >> 1);
  }
  h = new Array(GLYPH_W + 2);
  for (let i = 0; i < h.length; i++) {
    // Halo column i sits over glyph column i-1, so it wants that column and
    // the two either side of it — i-2, i-1 and i in glyph coordinates.
    h[i] = (i >= 2 ? smeared[i - 2] : 0)
      | (i >= 1 && i - 1 < GLYPH_W ? smeared[i - 1] : 0)
      | (i < GLYPH_W ? smeared[i] : 0);
  }
  halos.set(ch, h);
  return h;
}
